episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Who is allowed to fix things?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down [Williams Lake Tribune] Love speaks loudly outweighing online hate at Williams Lake Pride Parade and South Cariboo residents won’t have access to their local emergency department overnight : My Cariboo Now, plus 1 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Who should be allowed to verify, audit, and fix the systems embedded in cultural spaces—from facial recognition at venues to AI watermarks on recordings to aging audio equipment in local halls? Topics include: Facial recognition surveillance at entertainment venues and corporate accountability, AI-generated content watermarking and digital provenance verification, Repairability and local ownership of aging versus proprietary audio equipment, Arts funding disclosure standards for AI-assisted work, The gap between technical solutions and practical compliance in small communities.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Chilcotin Partners for Literacy

discussion.central_question: Who should be allowed to verify, audit, and fix the systems embedded in cultural spaces—from facial recognition at venues to AI watermarks on recordings to aging audio equipment in local halls?
discussion.riley_position: Communities should focus on local problems they can actually solve without external permission, particularly maintaining ownership and repairability of their own equipment and establishing simple disclosure standards for AI-assisted work.
riley_key_evidence: Analog mixing boards in Williams Lake venues remain repairable by local technicians while digital boards require manufacturer support from provinces away
Rural arts councils lack resources to become AI-provenance auditors, making technical solutions impractical for small venues
A one-line self-reported disclosure on funding applications costs little and puts the question on record without requiring independent verification
discussion.casey_position: The underlying trust problem is identical across all scales—from MSG's facial recognition to Google's SynthID watermarks to venue equipment—but the stakes and solutions differ, and small communities shouldn't pretend they can solve surveillance capitalism problems meant for legislators.
casey_key_evidence: Google's invisible SynthID watermark technically functions but requires active user effort to verify, making accountability theoretical rather than practical
MSG's facial recognition covers three major venues and affects thousands of people daily with no public oversight or consent mechanism
Album release dates cause a 15% jump in traffic deaths, showing systems are built by people disconnected from downstream consequences
discussion.resolution: Riley and Casey agreed that communities should implement a concrete, doable step—posting plain disclosure lines about AI-generated content in local recordings—while acknowledging this doesn't address larger surveillance governance issues that require legislative action beyond their scope.
